guideTitle: Best RV Air Conditioners for Pop-Up Campers (2026)
metaTitle: Best RV Air Conditioners for Pop-Up Campers
metaDescription: Six cooling units for pop-up campers compared on weight, wattage, window and tent fit, and which options a canvas-sided camper and its small battery can handle.
expertTake: The CYMYYDS 2700 BTU portable is the pick for a pop-up on a 15 amp circuit or a small power station, with a rated draw of just 280 watts. The COSTWAY 6500 BTU window unit is the step up when you have hookups and want real capacity. Skip any heavy rooftop unit, because a pop-up roof is a lifting canvas-and-aluminum structure that was never built to carry it.
introParagraphs: A pop-up camper turns the whole air conditioning question upside down. The roof lifts, the sides are canvas or soft panels, and the structure cannot carry a heavy rooftop unit. The space is small but leaky, and the power supply is often a basic circuit or a modest battery.

That leaves three practical forms: a portable unit that sits on the floor and vents through a window, a window-style unit that sits in an opening, and a compact battery-voltage unit for the few pop-ups with a rigid roof section. We rank each on weight, wattage and how well it works with a soft-sided shell.

products.name: CYMYYDS 2,700 BTU portable RV AC, 280W rated draw
products.description:
At a rated 280 watts, this unit asks for less than a hair dryer, which makes it the one air conditioner on this list that a basic pop-up circuit or a mid-size power station can feed without drama. The maker says it uses a real compressor, not an evaporative cooler, and quotes 2,700 BTU, about 900 watts of cooling.

That is a small amount of cold, and it matters how you use it. In a pop-up with canvas sides it will cool a sleeping area or a bunk end, not the whole camper, and it works best with the openings sealed and the unit pointed at the bed. The sleep mode is quoted at 45 dB, quiet enough for a tent-like space.

Against the larger units here it trades capacity for the lowest electrical demand. Vent the hose out a window panel, drain it as the maker directs and store it dry between trips.
products.bestFor: Pop-ups on a basic circuit or power station that need sleeping-zone cooling.
pros: Real compressor, not an evaporative cooler
cons: 2,700 BTU only cools a small zone
Needs an exhaust hose through a panel

products.name: COSTWAY 6,500 BTU RV window AC with WiFi and voice control
products.description:
A window-style unit needs an opening, and many pop-ups have one in the front or rear wall. The COSTWAY is sold as an RV window air conditioner with 6,500 BTU of cooling, ETL certification and WiFi plus voice control, which puts real capacity in a camper that has a rigid frame to hold it.

The weight sits at the window, not the roof, so the structure is not asked to carry it overhead. A 24 hour timer and cooling, fan and other modes round out the controls. It needs a panel or a custom insert to seal the opening, and a canvas-sided camper may need extra bracing.

Compared with the CYMYYDS it gives more than twice the capacity but draws much more power, so it wants hookups or a large battery system. Check the gasket and the drain tube every season and remove it for travel.
products.bestFor: Pop-ups with hookups and a rigid window opening.
pros: 6,500 BTU is real capacity for a small camper
Weight sits at the window, not the roof
cons: Needs a sealed opening and extra bracing on soft walls
Draws far more power than portable units

products.name: 7,000 BTU portable tent AC, 4-in-1, compact
products.description:
This portable unit is sold for tents, which makes it a natural fit for a pop-up's soft shell. It measures about 21 by 12 by 14 inches, small enough to sit on the floor beside a bunk, and the maker quotes 7,000 BTU of cooling with cool, dry, sleep, fan and timer modes.

The sleep mode is claimed at 58 dB, louder than the 45 dB CYMYYDS, so it is a trade of capacity for noise. Because it is compact and remote-controlled, it can be pointed at the bed from across the camper. As with any portable, the exhaust hose needs a path through a window or panel.

Compared with the COSTWAY it avoids the window mount but uses floor space. Seal around the hose, drain the condensate as directed and let the unit dry before storing it.
products.bestFor: Soft-sided pop-ups wanting more capacity than a mini portable.
pros: Compact body around 21 by 12 by 14 inches
Designed for tent and camper use
cons: 58 dB sleep mode is louder than the smallest unit
Needs a hose path and floor space

products.name: TURBRO inverter under-bench RV AC with heat pump, 115V
products.description:
For pop-ups that have a hard-sided dinette or storage bench, an under-bench inverter unit moves the weight to the floor. TURBRO's version uses an inverter compressor and a heat pump, keeps the roof clear and avoids any cut in the lift-up top.

The layout asks for an exhaust path and a drain, and it needs a bench with the space and airflow it requires. A soft-sided pop-up with a thin floor may not offer that, so check the frame. Inverter control keeps the draw modest at a steady setpoint.

Compared with the portables it is a permanent installation with real capacity and heat. Keep the intake clear, check the drain route and inspect connections after the first trip.
products.bestFor: Pop-ups with a rigid bench and no spare roof structure.
pros: Weight sits on the floor, not the roof
No cut in the lift-up top
cons: Needs a bench with space, exhaust and drain

products.name: 12V 8,500 BTU low-profile rooftop RV AC, variable frequency
products.description:
A few pop-ups, particularly hard-top conversions, have a roof that can carry a small unit. For those, this 12V low-profile model offers 8,500 BTU of cooling and 3,400 BTU of heating with a variable-frequency compressor, which modulates instead of cycling.

It runs on battery voltage, so it suits a pop-up with a solar and lithium setup. The low profile helps because a pop-up often tucks under low branches. The roof, however, must be rigid and reinforced, and an ordinary lift-up top cannot take it.

Against the portables it is a fixed installation with a higher draw and more cooling. Use heavy cable, a fuse and a low-voltage cutoff, and check the seal every spring.
products.bestFor: Hard-top pop-ups with solar and a lithium bank.

products.name: Xenjum 12V 11,000 BTU RV AC with heater, 43 lb
products.description:
If a pop-up has any rigid roof section, weight is the limiting factor, and at about 43 pounds the Xenjum is a fraction of a typical rooftop unit. It runs on 12V DC with an inverter scroll compressor and offers 11,000 BTU of cooling plus a 4,500 BTU heater.

That is more cooling than a small pop-up needs, so it will cycle less and run gently. A 35 dB claim for the quietest mode suits sleeping. But it still has to mount on a rigid, reinforced structure, which a standard lift-up roof is not.

Compared with the 8,500 BTU unit it has more capacity and weight to match. Run heavy cable with a fuse and a low-voltage cutoff, and inspect the roof seal and the structure every season.
products.bestFor: Rigid-roof campers that want the lightest 12V unit.
pros: Roughly 43 lb is easy on a small roof
cons: More capacity than a tiny camper needs

buyingCriteria.explanation: A pop-up's roof lifts on cranks or struts and its sides are canvas or thin panels. A rooftop unit weighs 70 pounds or more, far beyond what a lift-up top can carry. Portable and window-style units move the weight to the floor or a rigid frame, which is why the CYMYYDS, tent unit and COSTWAY lead this list.

Many pop-up campers have a 15 or 20 amp circuit or a modest power station. The CYMYYDS draws a rated 280 watts, easy on either. A 6,500 BTU window unit draws far more, so check your supply. Match the unit to the circuit before buying, because a tripped breaker at midnight is no relief.

Canvas sides leak cold air and let in heat, so any air conditioner works against a leaky envelope. Seal the openings, close the vents and use reflective covers on the sunniest wall. A small unit in a sealed sleeping zone beats a big unit in an open tent.

Portables need an exhaust hose through a window or panel and a way to handle condensate. A tight panel around the hose stops hot air coming back in. The 7,000 BTU tent unit and the CYMYYDS both need this, so plan the panel before the first trip.

A pop-up is a small sound box, so noise is amplified. Claims run from 35 dB on the Xenjum to 45 dB on the CYMYYDS and 58 dB on the 7,000 BTU unit in sleep mode. Those are quietest-mode figures. Place the unit away from your head and on a soft mat. A folded towel under the base and a clear gap between the unit and the canvas stop the hum from traveling through the floor frame and the walls.

A pop-up has a small volume, so 2,700 to 7,000 BTU often suffices. An oversized unit short-cycles and leaves the air clammy. Use the smallest unit that holds your target temperature, and add shade and reflective covers before stepping up in size. A thermometer by the bed tells you more than any coverage claim on a box.

howWeEvaluated.title: Structural fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged whether each unit puts weight on a roof, a window or the floor, and whether a pop-up can carry it. Portable and window units scored best for lift-up campers. Rooftop units were limited to rigid-roof conversions.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power demand
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated draw, from the CYMYYDS's 280 watts to the larger 115V units. Lower draw suits basic circuits and power stations. Inverter designs earned credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise claims
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the 35 dB Xenjum, the 45 dB CYMYYDS and the 58 dB tent unit as maker claims. A pop-up amplifies sound, so quiet mattered. We did not treat claims as measurements.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity versus volume
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched 2,700 to 11,000 BTU to a small pop-up volume. An oversized unit loses points for short cycling, which a small pop-up cabin invites. The smaller portables scored for right-sizing.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at hose paths, drains, panels and how easily each unit stows. Portables scored for flexibility. Permanent installs were flagged as projects.

maintenance.why: Standing water grows biofilm and smells. Drain the tank and let the unit dry before storing, and wipe the drain port so no residue hardens there between trips.

maintenance.task: Inspect the exhaust hose and panel
maintenance.why: A loose hose or gap lets hot air back in. A tight panel makes the unit work far better.
A small unit has little airflow margin. A clogged filter ices the coil.
A flattened gasket leaks cold air and rain. Replace it when it no longer springs back.
High-current lugs loosen. A warm terminal wastes power and is a fire risk.

faq.q: Can a pop-up camper take a rooftop air conditioner?
faq.a: Usually not. A lift-up roof is not built to carry 70 pounds or more. Only hard-top conversions with a reinforced roof can, and then a light unit like the Xenjum is best. Even then, have the roof structure checked, because a lifting mechanism and a fixed weight make poor partners and the failure shows up as a sagging ceiling.

faq.q: How much air conditioning does a pop-up need?
faq.a: Often 2,700 to 7,000 BTU is enough, because the volume is small. A leaky canvas shell is the bigger problem, so seal it and shade it first, and treat the air conditioner as the last piece of a cooling plan rather than the first. A reflective cover over the canvas on the sunny side, tightly zipped flaps, a ground cloth to reduce radiated heat from the sun-baked soil and a floor mat to cut ground heat can matter more than another thousand BTU of capacity.

faq.q: Will a portable unit run on a power station?
faq.a: A low-draw unit like the CYMYYDS, rated 280 watts, can on a mid-size station for a limited time. Check the station's output and capacity before relying on it. A 1,000 watt-hour station running a 280 watt unit gives roughly three hours at best, so plan on a larger station or a charging source for a full night.

faq.q: Do I need an exhaust hose?
faq.a: Yes for portables. The hose carries hot air out through a window or panel. A tight seal around it matters as much as the unit. Keep the hose short and straight, since every extra bend and every foot of length reduces the exhaust airflow and lets the hose itself radiate heat back into the room.

faq.q: Is a window unit better than a portable?
faq.a: It gives more capacity and uses no floor space, but needs a rigid opening and bracing. A portable is more flexible and draws less power. If your camper has no good opening, or you rent it out, the portable is the safer choice since it needs no alteration to the structure.

Yes on shore power. On a battery, run it at low speed in a sealed zone and use a low-voltage cutoff. Pre-cooling in the evening helps, and so does setting a timer so the unit drops out once the night air is cool enough, which also spares the battery and the compressor.
